slides.title: Why Invasions Came
slides.kicker: Wealth of the plains invited trouble
bullets: From the 7th century onwards, successive phases of invasions hit the subcontinent, driven by territorial expansion and religious motives.
The surplus agrarian produce of fertile plains, fed by perennial river systems, gave people economic well-being.
That very prosperity became a major reason for the invasions.
Against this backdrop, strategic alliances and confederacies emerged at regional and pan-Indian levels.
slides.note: Fertile plains full of grain, sabki nazar wahan!

slides.title: Arabs Turned Back
slides.kicker: Mid-7th century: attacks by sea and land
bullets: From the mid-7th century, Arab forces launched invasions by sea and land.
Indian rulers across the Deccan, Malwa, Kashmir and Rajasthan confronted and repulsed these early invaders.
This early wall of resistance stopped the first wave of attackers.

items: Arab invasions by sea and land
Rulers of Deccan, Malwa, Kashmir, Rajasthan

slides.note: Pehli line of defence held strong.

slides.title: Ghazni Strikes First
bullets: Mahmud, Sultan of Ghazni in present-day Afghanistan and northeastern Iran, launched his first invasion in 1001.
His target was Jayapala of the Hindu Shahi dynasty.
Through the 11th and 12th centuries, the Hindu Shahis, Chandellas, Solankis and Chauhans opposed and fought the Turkish invaders.
slides.note: Ghazni was in today's Afghanistan-Iran region.

slides.title: Who Held, Who Fell
bullets: In 1178, Queen Naiki Devi of the Chaulukya kingdom defeated Muhammad Ghuri at Kasahrada, near Mount Abu.
The Chauhans, Gahadavalas and Senas came under Turkic control towards the end of the 12th century.
Gujarat, Malwa and Bundelkhand under the Chandellas put up stiff resistance for about a hundred years thereafter.
The Turks failed to conquer present-day Odisha and parts of Assam; Rajputana states stayed centres of sustained resistance.

left.title: Held the line
items: Odisha and parts of Assam never taken

slides.note: North and west bore the brunt; the south stayed free.

slides.title: Kumbha Builds the Shield
bullets: Maharana Kumbha of Mewar consolidated a resistance framework between 1433 and 1468.
A key part of this framework was the construction of forts.
These strong foundations readied Mewar for the storms that followed.
slides.note: Pehle deewar, phir ladai!

slides.title: Siege of Chittor
bullets: Akbar, whose empire was then at the peak of its power, attacked Mewar and laid siege to the fort at Chittor in 1567-1568.
Under Rana Udai Singh, the Rajputs resisted for more than five months before the fort was captured.
The Mughal army paid a heavy price in the campaign.
In a strategic move, Udai Singh retreated to the Aravalli Hills with a large number of his subjects.

items: Rajputs resist for over five months
Fort captured; Udai Singh moves to the Aravalli Hills

slides.note: Retreat bhi ek strategy hoti hai.

slides.title: Haldighati to Guerrilla War
bullets: In 1576 Akbar attacked Mewar again; Maharana Pratap, son and successor of Udai Singh, fought the Mughals at Haldighati.
Pratap modified his military strategy and adopted guerrilla warfare.
He used the rugged Aravalli terrain for surprise attacks, raids and ambushes on the Mughal forces and their networks.
He continued to resist and eventually reclaimed most of his ancestral territories in the 1580s.

right.title: Guerrilla warfare
items: Rugged Aravalli terrain as an ally
Strikes on Mughal forces and their networks

slides.note: Pahad hi saathi ban gaye.

slides.title: Victory at Dewair
bullets: The Battle of Dewair, fought near Udaipur in 1582, was a turning point for Mewar.
It caused the collapse of key Mughal military outposts in Mewar.
It helped Maharana Pratap reclaim control over Mewar.
A victory memorial still stands at Dewair in Rajasthan.
slides.note: Victory memorial wahan aaj bhi khada hai.

slides.title: Amar Singh Holds the Line
bullets: Maharana Amar Singh, son and successor of Pratap, continued Mewar's tradition of military resistance against the Mughals.
Jahangir made military advances towards Mewar in 1605, 1608 and 1609.
Each attempt was countered by strong and organised resistance from the Rajputs.
Eventually the Mughals were compelled to acknowledge Mewar's distinct political position.
slides.note: Teen koshish, teen baar failure.

slides.title: Pressure on the South
bullets: Resistance to foreign invasions was not confined to northern India.
The expanding campaigns of the Delhi Sultanate steadily weakened the older kingdoms of the south.
Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khilji's general, attacked major cities and temples including Warangal, Belur and Madurai.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rise pushed the Sultanate farther south, contributing to the decline of the Pandya Kingdom.

items: Malik Kafur raids Warangal, Belur, Madurai

slides.note: The south was fighting its own fires.

slides.title: City of Victory, 1336
bullets: In 1336 the Vijayanagara Empire rose to check the expansion of the Sultanate into peninsular India.
Harihara and Bukka established the independent kingdom of Vijayanagara, meaning City of Victory.
It was located near present-day Hampi in Karnataka.
A formidable river and rugged, rocky terrain gave it strong natural defence and a secure base for military operations.
slides.note: The name says it all: Vijayanagara!

slides.title: Wealth in Four Languages
slides.kicker: Trade, culture, power by the rivers
bullets: The empire expanded by annexing territory south of the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.
It became one of the richest and most influential states of its time.
Literature flourished in Kannada, Telugu, Tamil and Sanskrit.
Its capital city became a centre of trade, culture and political power in southern India.
slides.note: Two rivers, one golden city.

slides.title: Tragedy at Kannanur
bullets: During Bukka's reign, Vijayanagara made major gains, subjugating the Madurai Sultanate and annexing Arcot.
In 1342 the ageing Hoysala king Vira Ballala III fought the Madurai Sultanate in the Battle of Kannanur.
The Sultan launched a surprise counter-attack and executed the Hoysala ruler.
For almost four decades, Vijayanagara wrestled with the Sultans of Madurai.

items: Vira Ballala III fights the Madurai Sultanate
Surprise counter-attack; the king is executed
Almost four decades of struggle follow

slides.note: One loss, but the fight was not over.

slides.title: Kampana Finishes the Fight
bullets: Kumara Kampana, the son of Bukka, led the campaign against the Madurai Sultanate.
He killed the Sultan and brought the Sultanate of Madurai to an end.
He reinstated the divine images in the Rajasimheshwara Temple at Kanchipuram and the Sri Ranganathaswamy Temple at Srirangam.
Later, in the 16th century, Krishnadevaraya took the empire to its peak, expanding and securing its dominance over the Deccan.

items: Divine images restored at Kanchipuram and Srirangam

slides.note: Temples of victory shone again.

slides.title: Rise of the Marathas
bullets: The Marathas were a formidable force in the Deccan, particularly during the 17th and 18th centuries.
The establishment of an independent Maratha state in 1674 is closely associated with the rise of Chhatrapati Shivaji.
Centuries of involvement in the region's politics gave them deep knowledge of the Deccan's complex geography and landscape.
Their bravery and martial abilities made them formidable in both administrative and military affairs.
slides.note: The Deccan's soil ran in their veins.

slides.title: The Spirit of Swarajya
bullets: In the Maratha state, territorial control and sovereignty were closely linked to the idea of swarajya, or self-rule.
Chhatrapati Shivaji is regarded as one of the earliest proponents of the spirit of Swarajya.
Swarajya meant an independent, self-governing territory free from external control.
slides.note: Apni zameen, apna raaj.

slides.title: Forts on the Hills
bullets: The Marathas strategically built forts such as Raigad and Sinhagad, which played a crucial role in resistance against the Mughals.
Their territory of hills and deep valleys made forts strategic nuclei for guerrilla warfare.
This network of forts enabled swift attacks from different directions and provided safe retreats.
Different types of forts were constructed to serve distinct purposes.

items: Forts built on hills like Raigad and Sinhagad

slides.note: Every hill hid a fort, every fort hid a plan.

slides.title: An Empire Run Ragged
slides.kicker: Aurangzeb: two decades in the Deccan
bullets: Prolonged warfare exhausted the Mughal Empire economically and politically.
Aurangzeb spent more than two decades in the Deccan trying to control the region and subdue Maratha resistance.
As political boundaries shifted, the Marathas relied on strategic alliances and built a vast network of tributary relationships.
This extended their influence far beyond areas under direct rule; bravery and military skills were the key to their success.

left.title: Mughal Empire
items: Aurangzeb: over two decades in the Deccan

slides.note: Mughals grew tired; Marathas grew stronger.

slides.title: Guru Nanak's Light
bullets: Guru Nanak founded a major spiritual movement in the late 15th century, which later came to be known as Sikhism.
It emphasised devotion to one God, social equality and the rejection of rituals.
Under Guru Nanak and his successors, the Sikh community expanded across the Punjab, Sindh and the Gangetic plains.
Punjab, then largely under the Lodi Sultans and later the Mughals, was fertile and densely populated.
slides.note: A small panth with a big heart.

slides.title: A Martyrdom Changes Everything
slides.kicker: Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru
bullets: From the beginning of the 17th century, the Mughal state increasingly intervened in the affairs of the Sikh Gurus.
Jahangir ordered the execution of Guru Arjan Dev on the pretext of the Guru's alleged support to his rebellious son, Khusrau Mirza.
The martyrdom marked a significant turning point in the history of the Sikhs.
It contributed to a gradual shift in their organisational and political orientation.

items: A turning point for the Sikhs

slides.note: One martyrdom, a whole community awakened.

slides.title: Akal Takht Rises
bullets: Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru, was detained by Jahangir in Gwalior Fort.
Sikhs visited Gwalior in large numbers and paid their respects to the Guru from outside the fortress.
Guru Hargobind established the Akal Takht, a seat of temporal authority, to administer justice and address matters of governance.
Many armed conflicts took place between the Sikhs and the Mughals.

items: Guru Hargobind detained in Gwalior Fort
Akal Takht established for justice and governance

slides.note: Spiritual strength now had a temporal seat.

slides.title: 1675: Faith Unbroken
bullets: In 1675, Aurangzeb ordered the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Sikh Guru; the martyrdom proved a turning point in Indian history.
The brutality against Guru Arjan Dev, Guru Tegh Bahadur and the tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, has few comparisons in history.
The valour and sacrifice of the Gurus became defining features of Sikhism.
Sikhs held that persecution had to be met with collective organisation and, as and when required, armed resistance.

items: Armed resistance as and when required

slides.note: Sacrifice made the conviction stronger.

examples.title: Mewar's timeline of defiance
examples.problem: Arrange Mewar's key acts of resistance between 1567 and 1609 in the correct order, naming the ruler and the event for each.
steps: Start with Akbar's siege of the Chittor fort in 1567-1568: Rajputs under Rana Udai Singh resisted for more than five months before the fort fell.
Next, in 1576 Akbar attacked Mewar again and Maharana Pratap fought the Mughal forces at the Battle of Haldighati.
Then comes the Battle of Dewair near Udaipur in 1582, which caused the collapse of key Mughal military outposts and helped Pratap reclaim control over Mewar.
Finally, Maharana Amar Singh countered Jahangir's military advances towards Mewar in 1605, 1608 and 1609.
examples.answer: 1567-1568 siege of Chittor under Udai Singh; 1576 Battle of Haldighati under Maharana Pratap; 1582 Battle of Dewair; 1605, 1608 and 1609 advances by Jahangir repelled by Amar Singh, after which the Mughals acknowledged Mewar's distinct political position.

examples.title: Who faced whom
examples.problem: Match each defender to the attacker they faced, using the chapter: Naiki Devi, Jayapala, Maharana Pratap, Kumara Kampana.
steps: Jayapala of the Hindu Shahi dynasty faced Mahmud of Ghazni's first invasion in 1001.
Naiki Devi of the Chaulukya kingdom defeated Muhammad Ghuri at Kasahrada near Mount Abu in 1178.
Maharana Pratap fought Akbar's Mughal forces at Haldighati in 1576, then used guerrilla warfare from the Aravalli Hills.
Kumara Kampana, son of Bukka, fought the Sultan of the Madurai Sultanate and killed him, ending that Sultanate.
examples.answer: Jayapala versus Mahmud of Ghazni (1001); Naiki Devi versus Muhammad Ghuri (1178); Maharana Pratap versus Akbar's Mughal forces (1576); Kumara Kampana versus the Madurai Sultan.

examples.title: Cause chain: why Vijayanagara rose
examples.problem: Build the cause chain that led to the founding of the Vijayanagara Empire in 1336.
steps: Malik Kafur, Alauddin Khilji's general, attacked major cities and temples including Warangal, Belur and Madurai.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq's rise to power extended the Delhi Sultanate's influence even farther south.
This contributed to the decline of the Pandya Kingdom and the emergence of the Madurai Sultanate.
Against this backdrop, Harihara and Bukka established Vijayanagara, the City of Victory, near present-day Hampi in 1336 to check the Sultanate's expansion into peninsular India.
examples.answer: Khilji-era raids, then Tughlaq-era expansion, then Pandya decline and the rise of the Madurai Sultanate, and finally the founding of Vijayanagara in 1336 as a check on the Sultanate.

examples.title: From martyrdom to organised resistance
examples.problem: Trace how Mughal pressure reshaped the Sikh community's organisation and outlook from the early 17th century to 1675.
steps: From the beginning of the 17th century, the Mughal state increasingly intervened in the affairs of the Sikh Gurus.
Jahangir ordered the execution of Guru Arjan Dev, the fifth Guru, on the pretext of his alleged support to Khusrau Mirza; this martyrdom marked a significant turning point.
Guru Hargobind, the sixth Guru, was detained in Gwalior Fort and later established the Akal Takht, a seat of temporal authority for justice and governance.
In 1675 Aurangzeb ordered the execution of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, firming the conviction that persecution had to be met with firm resistance and resilience.
examples.answer: The martyrdoms of Guru Arjan Dev under Jahangir and Guru Tegh Bahadur under Aurangzeb in 1675 shifted the Sikhs towards collective organisation and armed resistance as and when required, with the Akal Takht anchoring temporal authority.
